newsitem.title: USA: Homeowner refinancing to prompt US bond mkt rally.
newsitem.headline: Homeowner refinancing to prompt US bond mkt rally.

text.p: U.S. homeowners face their best chance to refinance mortgages since early 1996. That would cut their costs, but hurt many investors holding securities backed by those home loans, housing analysts said.

A rally that boosts 10-year Treasuries just about a point and is sustained for several weeks would ignite that refinancing wave. As homeowners lock in lower rates, mortgage-backed securities (MBS) prepay early, cutting off cash streams and forcing holders to reinvest at lower yields.
In a self-feeding cycle, many investors would then dump MBS and seek haven in Treasuries, helping Treasuries rally further and making prepayments an even greater risk, analysts agreed.
"We feel that there is going to be a mortgage-driven Treasury rally," said Dale Westhoff, senior managing director and head of mortgage research at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc.

There were other prepay chances in February and last December. However, both were too brief for many homeowners to act, he said. "We think this (bond) rally has a lot of legs, as opposed to other times we've rallied this year."

Investors have already been selling high-coupon MBS and swapping into discount MBS, which are insulated from early prepayments. Discount bonds have gotten more costly as a result, making Treasuries a viable alternative.

High-coupon and interest-only mortgage securities are hurt most by prepayments. MBS are prepaid at par. That creates losses for 8.00 percent and higher coupons that trade three to about 10 points above par. Holders of bonds that pay only interest would see their cash stream evaporate entirely.
Ten-year Treasury note yields need only drop to 6.10 percent, from 6.22 percent Wednesday, to unleash the pent-up home refinancing spree, several mortgage analysts said.

Treasury 10-year and 30-year bonds have been hovering around their lowest yields since December 1996. With inflation contained and Federal Reserve monetary policy on hold, Treasury analysts also doubted the rally will quit soon.

However, no one predicted a repeat of the exodus that plagued mortgage securities earlier this decade, when some holders got their shirts handed to them as interest rates plunged to 20-year lows. Homeowners refinanced en-masse in 1992 and 1993, creating massive MBS losses.
Portfolio managers and analysts said MBS investors and their debt monitoring systems were now more sophisticated.
Consequently, "Panics don't exist," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.
Michael Miller, vice president at Prudential Securities Inc, agreed, saying the days of purely mortgage-driven Treasury rallies are over.

"The Street is more conscious of the negative convexity of mortgages and are better at managing the risk than they were two years ago, so there's less mass exodus from mortgages as the market trades up," he said.

Nonetheless, a 10-year Treasury yield below 6.00 percent was widely viewed as a psychological trigger for escalated prepayments. A drop to the 5.75-percent level could seriously alter the MBS landscape, most analysts agreed, although none of them predicted such a dramatic rate slide.

Michael Hoeh, vice president and senior portfolio manager at Dreyfus Corp, said, "It doesn't look like the consumer is all that alerted to the potential" for refinancing their home loans. The rate decline has occurred swiftly, and it usually takes time to trickle through to the consumer level.

Although prepayments will accelerate, "I'm not all that bullish on the market," he said. "I don't see it rallying another 30-40 basis points. It would have to rally more than 20 basis points for any real fear to take place."
Pools of refinancable mortgage securities are signficant, however. Bonds issued in 1994-1997, after the last major prepay fest, were particularly sensitive, analysts said.
Bear Stearns estimated that $140 million of 30-year 8.0-percent through 9.0-percent MBS were outstanding.
The larger threat is the 7 1/2-percent coupon. There are $267 billion in outstanding 30-year 7-1/2-percent mortgage securities, Bear Stearns said.

"That coupon alone represents 24 percent of the entire mortgage market," Westhoff stated. "My feeling is that the 7-1/2-percent coupon is what separates us from the 1993 scenario," he said, referring to the prepay barrage that year. Ten-year Treasury yields fell to around 5.25 percent in 1993.

"Almost every large mortgage investor has a fairly significant exposure to the 7-1/2 coupon," he added. If 10-year Treasury yields fall 40-50 basis points, "it's just a watershed event" for mortgage securities, Westhoff predicted.
